title: Performance interview sprint card — the 30-second answer, the numbers to memorise, and follow-up prep
body: > This is the pocket version of [#90](/blog?post=90): the thing to read the night before an interview — conclusions only, no reasoning. The number after each line is where to read more. ## The 30-second version > Take a baseline first and wire up RUM. Do the hygiene checklist unconditionally. Diagnose field first, then lab, and produce one sentence: "which page, which users, which metric, stuck at which stage". Route by that sentence — delivery layer, server layer or code layer. Inside the code layer, work in the order loading, requests, node count, where state lives, rendering, one change at a time. Finally, gate it in CI and alert on RUM so it does not slide back. The closing line: **the order of performance work is not "which layer to start from"; it is "first know which layer the problem is in".** ## Five steps, one keyword each | Step | Keyword | One line | See | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | **Baseline** | Have the numbers before you change anything, or you cannot prove it | #90 | | 1 | **Hygiene** | Compression, hash + long cache, no full-import dependencies, no lazy on the LCP image, production build | #69 #67 | | 2 | **Diagnose** | Field says "how many", attribution says "which stage", lab says "which line" | #64 #66 #62 | | 3 | **Route** | Bad INP → code layer, bad LCP → delivery layer, high TTFB → server layer | #90 | | 4 | **Fix** | loading → requests → node count → where state lives → rendering; `memo` last | #73 | | 5 | **Lock in** | size-limit, Lighthouse CI assertions, p75 alerts | #64 #70 | ## Numbers to memorise | Metric | Good / poor | Notes | |---|---|---| | LCP | ≤ 2.5s / > 4s | Four stages: TTFB → resource load delay → resource load duration → element render delay; **the second stage is where things most often go wrong** | | INP | ≤ 200ms / > 500ms | Three segments: input delay → processing → presentation; close to the worst interaction, not the average | | CLS | ≤ 0.1 / > 0.25 | The largest session window, not a running total | | TTFB | ≤ 800ms | Includes redirects, DNS, TLS; slow ≠ slow backend — split it with `Server-Timing` | | Long task | > 50ms | Main thread held for more than 50ms | | CrUX | p75, 28-day rolling, Chrome only, traffic threshold | After a change ships, 2–4 weeks before it shows | | Lighthouse weights | TBT 30%, LCP 25%, CLS 25% | FID retired 2024-03, TTI retired in Lighthouse 10 | | First-load JS | 30–120 KB gzipped is acceptable | This site's three chunks: 32 / 50 / 40 KB | ## Follow-up prep - **"Lighthouse went up but production didn't move?"** — Lab is one simulated run, field is a distribution. The classic failure: the test environment's APIs were mocked and the bottleneck was the API. - **"Why does `memo` come last?"** — Loading 300KB less saves hundreds of milliseconds; cutting one render saves a few. But that is an LCP statement; in an INP problem a single re-render of 3000 nodes taking 400ms *is* the cause, and the order flips. - **"How do you debug bad INP?"** — In production, `web-vitals/attribution` gives `interactionTarget`, the three-segment split and `longestScript`; locally, the Interactions track in the Performance panel with 4x CPU throttling to reproduce. TBT is only a load-time proxy and cannot see post-load interactions. - **"What if LCP is an image?"** — Discovery timing before size: `` not a CSS background, `fetchpriority="high"`, `preload`, and never `loading="lazy"`. Compression is third; sizing to fit and going lossy are the big wins. - **"Does splitting help a single-entry app?"** — Yes, but the goal is cache stability and parallel download, not de-duplication or a smaller total. webpack needs `chunks: 'all'`; Vite uses `manualChunks`. If the output is already small, don't split. - **"Does route-level lazy loading have a cost?"** — One extra round trip on navigation, covered by hover prefetching: `onMouseEnter={() => import(...)}`. - **"How do you prove the optimisation worked?"** — Baseline before, same-profile re-run after; in production wait out the 28-day window, or compare by the release / rollout-batch dimension in RUM. CrUX cannot separate A/B groups. - **"Why build an SDK when web-vitals exists?"** — web-vitals is the metric-calculation layer; transport, sampling, SPA route attribution and error correlation are left open. The reason to build is context: business line, route pattern, rollout batch, and "business-ready ≠ LCP". In one line: what you buy does not know your business. - **"What does SSR improve?"** — FCP / LCP, the bundle (RSC), request waterfalls. TTFB and server cost get worse; INP is unchanged. Do not say SSR improves TTI. ## Five wrong answers to avoid 1. Compressing images for bad INP, wrapping in `memo` for bad LCP. 2. Lab before field; reporting a Lighthouse 90. 3. Putting splitting and route-level lazy loading on the "unconditional" list. 4. Saying useEffect always runs after paint, or that a click's setState goes through the Scheduler. 5. Calling FID or TTI core metrics. ## The "have you done it" dimension - This site's Lighthouse run: LCP 6.8s but CLS 0.001 and TBT 30ms → the whole problem was the first-load chain; the top suggestion was render-blocking resources, estimated saving 470ms. → #62 - 58 screenshots, 23.7 MB, converted to lossy WebP at 2.4 MB, 9.8x — the bulk of it from going lossy, not from the format. → #65 - Virtualised list: DOM from 500+ to a constant dozen or so, 30 → 60 FPS. → the library write-up, #21 ## Related - The full framework: [#90](/blog?post=90) · the five code-level layers: [#73](/blog?post=73) · metrics: [#63](/blog?post=63) · toolchain: [#62](/blog?post=62)
